title: Image layers and build cache
description: Understand how Docker images are built from layers, how the build cache works, and how to write Dockerfiles that produce fast, small, and secure images.

data.text: Every Docker image is built from stacked read-only layers, and Docker's build cache is one of the most powerful tools for making image builds fast. In this lesson, you will learn exactly how layers are created, why cache invalidation happens, and how to write Dockerfiles that reuse work instead of rebuilding it on every build.

Docker images are not a single file. They are a stack of read-only layers, each generated by one instruction in your Dockerfile. When Docker builds an image, it runs one instruction at a time. If the input files for that instruction have not changed since the last build, Docker reuses the existing layer from its cache instead of running the command again. This is the build cache.

data.title: Layer facts
data.text: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a new layer. `FROM`, `RUN`, `COPY`, and `ADD` are all layer-producing instructions. Environment variables set with `ENV` also create layers.

The order of instructions matters a great deal. Docker invalidates the cache for an instruction and every instruction after it whenever any input to that instruction changes. The most common inputs are: files copied with `COPY` or `ADD`, files referenced by `RUN` commands, and the base image declared by `FROM`. A small change at the top of a Dockerfile can invalidate dozens of cached layers below it.

A cache-friendly Dockerfile puts the most stable parts of the build first and the most volatile parts last. Dependencies rarely change, so install them early. Application code changes on almost every commit, so copy it last.

data.title: Cache-friendly Node.js Dockerfile
data.content: This Dockerfile copies only the dependency manifest first, installs dependencies, and only then copies the rest of the application. Every time application code changes, the `npm install` layer is still reused.
data.code:
FROM node:20-slim

WORKDIR /app

# 1. Copy dependency manifest first
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# 2. Install dependencies (cached unless package.json changes)
RUN npm ci --production

# 3. Copy application code last
COPY . .

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

data.title: What breaks the build cache
items: Copying the entire project directory before installing dependencies
Running `apt-get update` and `apt-get install` in the same layer, which means every apt metadata change invalidates the installed packages
Using `ADD` for local files when `COPY` is clearer and more predictable
Building with a different base image tag than before, which invalidates every layer below the `FROM` instruction
Running package managers without their lock files, causing dependency resolution to change on every build

data.title: Watch out for cache poisoning
data.text: If you pin a base image to a floating tag like `latest`, your build cache is unpredictable. Use immutable digests or fixed minor-version tags such as `node:20.18.0-slim` to keep builds reproducible.

Even when the cache is working well, large intermediate layers can slow down pushes, pulls, and deployments. Every `RUN` instruction that creates files should clean up package manager caches and temporary artifacts in the same instruction. Otherwise those files become part of the final image layer, even if they are deleted in a later step.

data.title: Cleaning up in a single RUN layer
data.content: On Debian-based images, remove apt caches in the same RUN instruction that installs packages. Otherwise the cache directory remains in the final image.
data.code:
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

data.text: Use `docker image history <image>` to see each layer and its size. If one layer is unexpectedly large, inspect the corresponding Dockerfile instruction. Common culprits are `COPY . .` when the project directory contains `node_modules`, build artifacts, or test fixtures.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Docker images are stacks of read-only layers created by Dockerfile instructions
The build cache reuses layers when their inputs have not changed
Order instructions from least volatile to most volatile to maximize cache hits
Clean up package caches and temp files inside the same RUN instruction that creates them
Pin base images to immutable tags or digests for reproducible builds
data.takeaway: Good Dockerfile order is the single most impactful optimization for build speed and image size.
